title: India Slashes Windfall Tax on Diesel and Jet Fuel Exports, Raises Petrol Levy From July 1
excerpt: Diesel export duty cut 39% to ₹8.50/litre and ATF duty slashed 40% as global oil prices ease, while petrol levy nearly triples to ensure domestic supply
body:
India has recalibrated its windfall tax regime on fuel exports, cutting levies on diesel and aviation turbine fuel (ATF) while raising the duty on petrol — a move that reflects the government's evolving response to a global oil market that has cooled significantly since the crisis peaks earlier this year.

The revised rates, announced by the Finance Ministry on Tuesday, will take effect from July 1. The export duty on diesel has been slashed to ₹8.50 per litre from ₹14, while the ATF levy drops to ₹7.50 per litre from ₹12.50. In contrast, the petrol export duty has been raised to ₹4 per litre from ₹1.50, as the government seeks to ensure adequate domestic supply of the fuel.

The changes will have no impact on domestic retail fuel prices, which are set separately.

## Why the Shift Now

The windfall tax adjustments are driven by a dramatic shift in the global oil landscape. Crude prices have fallen sharply from peaks above $126 per barrel seen during the height of the West Asia crisis, when the US-Israel conflict with Iran and sweeping retaliatory strikes disrupted supply chains and sent markets into a frenzy. The easing of geopolitical tensions and the restoration of shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz have calmed fears of prolonged supply disruptions.

Economists and analysts now forecast that Brent crude will average $84.50 per barrel in 2026, down from projections of $90.44 just last month. That declining trajectory has given India room to ease the export levies that were originally imposed as emergency measures to prevent domestic shortages.



> **"Economists and analysts now forecast that Brent crude will average $84.50 per barrel in 2026, down from projections of $90.44 just last month."**


The windfall taxes — formally classified as Special Additional Excise Duty (SAED) and Road and Infrastructure Cess (RIC) — were first introduced on March 27, 2026, targeting diesel and ATF exports in the backdrop of the West Asia crisis. On May 16, the regime was extended to include petrol exports. The rates have been revised on a fortnightly basis since then, with the previous adjustment taking effect on June 16, when diesel and ATF duties were actually hiked.

## The Strategic Calculus


![Finance Ministry — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cd/Government-Vedder-Highsmith-detail-1.jpeg)


The differential treatment of fuels reveals the government's strategic priorities. Diesel and ATF, which saw their export duties cut by 39% and 40% respectively, are commodities where India has considerable refining surplus. Major refiners like Reliance Industries (which operates the world's largest refining complex at Jamnagar) and Indian Oil Corporation have been significant exporters, and the high duties were eating into their margins even as global prices fell.

Petrol, however, tells a different story. Domestic demand for petrol has remained robust, driven by India's growing passenger vehicle fleet and limited public transport alternatives in many cities. The government's decision to nearly triple the petrol export levy signals its intent to keep more petrol at home, even as it relaxes constraints on diesel and jet fuel.

The Finance Ministry also expanded exemptions for fuel exports made by public sector oil companies to Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka. In a notable addition, exports to Mauritius and Maldives have now been included in the exemption list — a move that strengthens India's diplomatic ties with Indian Ocean neighbours while maintaining its neighbourhood-first energy diplomacy.

## Market Impact and Refiner Relief

The relief for refiners is substantial. Indian refining stocks had come under pressure as the windfall taxes squeezed export margins, even as crude input costs eased. The reduction in diesel and ATF export duties is expected to improve profitability for companies across the refining chain, particularly Reliance Industries, Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum, and Hindustan Petroleum.

India's refining capacity of approximately 254 million tonnes per annum significantly exceeds domestic consumption, making fuel exports a major revenue earner. The country exported refined petroleum products worth over $70 billion in FY26, and the windfall tax regime has been a key variable in determining how much of that trade remains economically viable.

## What It Means for Consumers and Investors

For Indian consumers, the immediate impact is nil — the windfall taxes apply only to exports and do not affect pump prices. However, the broader signal matters. The fact that global crude prices are declining means the pressure on India's oil import bill is easing, which is positive for the current account deficit, the rupee, and inflation.

For NRI investors with exposure to Indian energy stocks, the diesel and ATF duty cuts are a clear positive for refining margins. The fortnightly revision mechanism means the rates could change again in mid-July, but the directional trend — lower duties as oil prices ease — is favorable.

The windfall tax regime, born of crisis, appears to be entering a phase of normalisation. Whether it survives as a permanent feature of India's fiscal architecture or is wound down entirely as oil markets stabilise will depend on how the geopolitical landscape evolves in the second half of 2026.
